chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Health hearing, asks everyone to silence electronic devices, and directs those wishing to testify to fill out a slip with the Sergeant at Arms. Staff also warns that no one may approach the front desk and then invites the Chair to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens Health Committee hearing and gives attendee instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Health.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Ladies and gentlemen, at this time, we please ask you to silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to fill out a testimony slip, then please see one of the sergeant arm officers.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, at no point in time has anyone to approach the front desk.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lynn Schulman opens the hearing as Chair and thanks colleagues and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene for attending. She notes that Council Members Marte, De La Rosa, Wilson, and Ariola are joining, with Ariola on Zoom.
chapters.title: Chair Schulman opens Health Committee hearing and welcomes attendees

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to today's hearing of the New York City Council Committee on Health.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Lynn Schulman, Chair of the Committee.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues and the representatives from the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene for joining us today to discuss food service establishment inspections in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We've been joined today by Councilmembers Marte,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: De La Rosa, Wilson, and Areola on Zoom.

chapters.summary: Schulman says public health means protecting New Yorkers in daily life, including safe food, consistent standards for businesses, and accessible health information. She says the committee will examine DOHMH oversight of food service inspections and consider related food safety, restaurant accountability, tobacco, disease prevention, and children's nutrition bills.
chapters.title: Schulman frames public health as everyday food safety and accountability

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: At its core, public health is about protecting New Yorkers in their everyday lives.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It means making sure the food we eat is safe, that the businesses serving our communities meet clear and consistent standards, and that New Yorkers have access to information that supports their health and well-being.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Today, the committee will examine DOHMH's oversight of food service establishment inspections and consider a range of legislation addressing food safety, restaurant accountability, tobacco regulation, disease prevention, and children's nutrition.

chapters.summary: Schulman cites Council analysis showing initial sanitary inspections fell from 99.5% of restaurants in FY2019 to 69.7% in FY2025. She attributes the drop to COVID-19 impacts on inspection rates and public health sanitarian staffing, though monthly inspections have recently increased.
chapters.title: Schulman presents inspection rate decline from FY2019 to FY2025

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The Council's analysis of DOHMH data in preparation for this hearing highlights the current challenges facing the city's restaurant inspection program.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2019, 99.5% of restaurants received an initial sanitary inspection.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: By fiscal year 2025, that figure had fallen to 69.7% and almost 30% drop.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The COVID-19 pandemic seriously impacted inspection rates and staffing levels for public health sanitarians.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: the title given to restaurant inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Recently, there are encouraging signs of increased inspection activity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The average number of monthly inspections rose from approximately 1,400 in the final quarter of 2023 to nearly 2,200 by June 2024, reaching just under 2,700 by August 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: However, the department's entry-level public health sanitarian workforce has not returned to its pre-COVID levels, and inspection trends reflect this reality.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: These data raise questions about staffing, inspection capacity, and the department's ability to provide consistent oversight across the city's food service establishments.

chapters.summary: Schulman says facility and equipment maintenance and pest presence and prevention account for nearly half of all violations. She argues this shows why routine inspections, accurate documentation, and timely corrective action are essential.
chapters.title: Schulman highlights top violation categories and need for routine inspections

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The Council's analysis also found that facility and equipment maintenance and pest presence and prevention account for nearly half of all violations across inspections.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: These findings underscore why routine inspections, accurate documentation, and timely corrective action are essential to protecting New Yorkers from unsafe and unsanitary conditions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We want to understand how DOHMH is addressing inspection capacity, prioritizing inspections and follow-up visits, and ensuring that violations are identified, documented, and corrected.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We look forward to DOHMH's engagement with these topics.

chapters.summary: Schulman says the committee will consider six introductions and one resolution, starting with proposals on restaurant operations, food safety, and accountability. She describes Intro 189-A on photographing violations, Intro 908 on digital certificate verification, and Intro 1124 on five-year food protection certificate renewal.
chapters.title: Schulman outlines restaurant inspection and food protection bills

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In addition, the committee will consider six introductions and one resolution.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: These three proposals today focus on restaurant operations, food safety, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Proposed Intro 189A, sponsored by Councilman...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Member Farias would require photographs or video documenting each cited violation when a restaurant inspection results in 14 or more points.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Intro 908, sponsored by Councilmember Santuso, would establish a digital system for verifying food protection certificates and prevent a restaurant from being penalized solely because a physical certificate is not present,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: provided the required certification can be verified as valid digitally.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: An intro 1124 sponsored by myself would require individuals managing or supervising food service establishments to renew their food protection course certification every five years.

chapters.summary: Schulman introduces Intro 405-A, which sets nutrition standards for children's meals at chain restaurants, and Intro 947, which would allow qualifying tobacco bars facing hardship to transfer registration and a retail dealer license once. She says DOHMH's perspective on tobacco licensing and public health implications will be important.
chapters.title: Schulman presents children's nutrition and tobacco bar bills

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We will also hear proposed Intro 405A and Intro 947, both sponsored by Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Healthy eating habits begin early, and the food and beverages children consume can have lasting implications for their health and development.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Proposed Intro 405A would establish nutrition standards for children's meals served at chain restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Intro 947 concerns tobacco bars.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The bill would allow a qualifying tobacco bar experiencing financial hardship to seek a one-time transfer of its registration and a one-time transfer

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: of its tobacco retail dealer license to a new location subject to specified conditions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing DOHMH's perspective on the public health implications of the proposal and how the existing registration and licensing framework for tobacco bars and tobacco restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: retail dealers operates.

chapters.summary: Schulman describes Intro 1094, requiring building owners to report Legionella test results of at least 10 CFU/mL to DOHMH, following a September hearing on Legionnaires' disease. She also introduces Resolution 152, supporting state legislation on certain food additives and color additives in schools.
chapters.title: Schulman introduces Legionella reporting bill and food additive resolution

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As a follow-up to our hearing on Legionnaire's disease this past September, we will also consider my legislation, Introduction 1094, requiring building owners to report Legionella test results of at least 10 colony-forming units per milliliter to DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Timely reporting of test results can be a critical component of identifying potential health risks, and giving DOHMH access to more testing data could help the agency take a more proactive approach.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The metric I am proposing in this bill was implemented in jurisdictions in Canada and has been a successful tool in proactively addressing Legionnaire's disease.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We want to understand how the proposed requirement would fit into DOHMH's existing practices and whether the agency sees a benefit to changing this reporting threshold.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Finally, we will hear Resolution 152, sponsored by Councilmember Stevens, supporting state legislation addressing certain food additives as well as color additives in food sold in schools.

chapters.summary: Schulman thanks colleagues for the proposals and DOHMH Deputy Commissioner Corinne Schiff for appearing. She says she looks forward to discussion on strengthening restaurant inspections, food safety, foodborne illness, and rebounding inspection rates.
chapters.title: Schulman thanks colleagues and DOHMH, previews discussion

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In closing, I want to thank my colleagues for bringing these proposals forward.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to thank Deputy Commissioner Corinne Schiff and DOHMH for appearing before the committee today.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I look forward to a substantive discussion about how we can strengthen restaurant inspection and enforcement practices, promote food safety, which we all know is really important these days.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Address and I want to thank the DOHMH who's been really on top of this issue.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So addressing emerging foodborne illness concerns and how we can collaborate to ensure that inspection rates rebound.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Together we can work

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: to improve these processes for restaurants, for the inspectors, and for the public.

chapters.summary: Schulman reads a statement from Council Member Santoso, sponsor of Intro 908, which would create a digital database of food protection certificate holders. Santoso says the bill closes a bureaucratic loophole that penalizes restaurants when a certified worker lacks a physical certificate, without changing food safety requirements.
chapters.title: Schulman reads Council Member Santoso statement on Intro 908

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: With that, I would like to read a brief statement by Councilmember Santantososo on her legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I would like to thank Councilmember Shulman for including Intro 908 onto today's agenda and the legislative staff, especially Christopher Pepe, for their work drafting this bill.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Intro 908 would close a bureaucratic loophole that is hurting beloved restaurants across our city.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Currently, any restaurant that is open for business

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: must have at least one person on site who holds a food protection certificate.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This is an important regulation that helps keep restaurants safe for patrons.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: However, when DOHMH conducts an inspection, the certified worker must have a physical copy of the certificate on hand.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Otherwise, the restaurant could receive a serious violation and hefty fine, despite DOHMH presumably having a database that shows who is certified.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So if a worker forgot to bring their certificate to work that day, the restaurant is penalized, despite the fact that this worker is a duly certified food protection worker.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation is very simple.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It would require DOHMH to create and maintain a digital database of food protection certificate holders and to consult that database during inspections if a worker does not have their certificate on hand.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This would not eliminate DOHMH's ability to enforce the underlying rule requiring certification in the first place and does not change food safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It simply recognizes that we are in an increasingly digital world and that checking a database is often a more

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: efficient system than requiring a worker to remember a physical card every day.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Passing this legislation would demonstrate to the hospital industry that the city supports them and wants to make it easier for them to continue serving our neighborhoods for years to come.

chapters.summary: Schulman reads a statement from Council Member Riley on Intro 405-A, the Healthy Kids Meals Bill, which would strengthen nutrition standards for children's meals at chain restaurants. Riley also discusses Intro 947, which would create a pathway for eligible tobacco bars facing financial hardship to relocate and resume operations under DOHMH oversight.
chapters.title: Schulman reads Council Member Riley statement on Intro 405 and 947

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Now I would like to read a brief statement by Councilmember Riley on his bills.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman and the committee for hearing two important pieces of legislation focused on the health of New Yorkers and supporting our local businesses.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: First, Intro 504A, the Healthy Kids Meals Bill.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As a father of three, I know firsthand how challenging it can be to make healthy choices for our children when dining out.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Families should not have to sacrifice their children's health for convenience, and healthy options should not depend on where a family lives or chooses to eat.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation establishes stronger nutrition standards for children's meals, including fruits, vegetables, healthier beverage options, and specific nutritional requirements for chain restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Our goal is simple.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Make healthier meals the standard, encourage good habits early, and give families greater confidence in the choices available to their children.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Next, Intro 947 addresses the operation of tobacco bars in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We recognize that longstanding businesses can face financial hardships that threaten their ability to remain operational.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This legislation creates a pathway for eligible, previously registered tobacco bars to relocate and resume operations subject to demonstrated financial hardship, Department of Health improvement, and applicable requirements.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's about balancing economic opportunity with economic opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: with responsible oversight and the interests of our communities.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I look forward to today's discussion and thank my colleagues, the legislative drafting team, and all stakeholders who have contributed to advancing these bills.

chapters.title: Committee administers oath and acknowledges Council Member Epstein

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And now I will ask our council to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may proceed with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Before we do that, I just want to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: Corinne Schiff introduces herself as Deputy Commissioner for Environmental Health and names colleagues Kim Kessler, Dr. Achala Talati, and Vasuda Reddy. She says she will testify on food safety, foodborne illness outbreaks, tobacco control, nutrition in restaurants, and cooling tower regulation.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Corinne Schiff introduces DOHMH team and testimony scope

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Schulman and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: My name is Corinne Schiff, and I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Environmental Health at the New York City Health Department.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'm joined today by Kim Kessler, Assistant Commissioner for the Bureau of Chronic Disease Prevention, by Dr.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Achala Talati, Director of Tobacco Policy and Programs, and by Vasuda Reddy, Deputy Director of the Bureau of Communicable Diseases.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: On behalf of Commissioner Martin, thank you for the opportunity to testify today about our program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Programs to promote food safety, address foodborne illness outbreaks, control tobacco, advance nutrition efforts in restaurants, and regulate operation of the city's cooling towers.

chapters.summary: Schiff says DOHMH permits restaurants, educates owners, trains supervisors, conducts unannounced inspections, and issues letter grades. She notes about 90% of restaurants currently post an A grade, and the department investigates food poisoning complaints and outbreaks such as the nationwide cyclospora outbreak.
chapters.title: Schiff describes DOHMH food safety inspection and grading program

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The Health Department is charged with protecting and promoting the health of all New Yorkers, including to promote the highest food safety standards in New York City restaurants, respond to foodborne illness outbreaks,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: reduce tobacco-related disease and death, encourage consumption of healthy foods, and promote compliance with the local law governing cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: To protect diners, the department issues permits, conducts outreach and education for restaurant owners, trains restaurant supervisors in food protection,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: conducts unannounced inspections, and issues inspection grades so New Yorkers and the millions who visit our city can make informed decisions about where to eat out.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: About 90% of restaurants are currently posting an A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department investigates complaints of food poisoning and conducts foodborne illness outbreak investigations.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: investigations, often working with public health experts across the country, as in the recent nationwide cyclospora outbreak.

chapters.summary: Schiff says New York City has long led in tobacco control through the Smoke-Free Air Act, which reduced smoking by over 50% since 2002. She ties continued tobacco prevention to Healthy NYC and a multi-agency chronic disease strategy, noting smoking remains a leading cause of death.
chapters.title: Schiff reviews tobacco control history and Healthy NYC chronic disease strategy

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The Health Department also implements a wide variety of measures to protect New Yorkers from the harms of smoking, and New York City has long been a leader in tobacco control.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The city's landmark Smoke-Free Air Act dramatically limited indoor smoking, making New York City a model for jurisdictions around the world, protecting New Yorkers from secondhand smoke, and normalizing a smoke-free culture.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The SFAA, along with other strategies, has enabled the city to reduce the smoking rate by over 50% since 2002, but smoking remains a leading cause of death and continues to be a public health priority.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The Council and the Department have continuously strengthened the City's tobacco retail and secondhand smoke policies.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Those efforts have paid off in expanded life expectancy and a reduction in tobacco-related diseases and deaths.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Most recently, Chair Schulman and the City Council codified Healthy NYC, the Department's plan for improving life expectancy and creating a healthier city for all.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Preventing tobacco use and reducing smoking among New Yorkers is critical to reducing, to reaching the chronic disease goals set under Healthy NYC and increasing life expectancy.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The Health Department also released a multi-agency strategy that addresses the root causes of chronic diseases, which are a leading cause of death in New York City, taking an especially high toll on Black New Yorkers and New Yorkers in communities experiencing disinvestment.

chapters.summary: Schiff describes DOHMH's cooling tower program: issuing regulations, conducting outreach and training, inspecting systems, and issuing summonses for noncompliance. She says the department also responds to Legionnaires' disease clusters by testing towers and requiring cleaning and disinfection.
chapters.title: Schiff outlines cooling tower oversight and Legionella response

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Finally, as discussed at a hearing last month, the department promotes compliance with the city's nation-leading requirements dictating the operation of cooling towers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We issue detailed regulations to implement the local law protections, conduct outreach, education, and training, and inspect cooling tower systems to monitor compliance, issuing summonses subject to civil penalties when owners fail to comply.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We also respond to community clusters of Legionnaire's disease, rapidly testing cooling towers and requiring owners to fully clean and disinfect to cut off the Legionella bacteria likely to be causing the cluster.

chapters.summary: Schiff explains that Intro 908 would require DOHMH to maintain and check a database of food protection certificate holders before enforcement. She says a trained supervisor on site is critical, but the department is concerned about maintaining decades of records; she supports the intent of Intro 1124's five-year renewal and wants to work with Council on details.
chapters.title: Schiff comments on Intro 908 FPC database and Intro 1124 recertification

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation under consideration today, Introduction 908 would require the department to maintain a database of food protection certificate holders and check it to confirm there is an FPC holder present

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: at the restaurant before taking enforcement action.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Having a supervisor trained in food protection on site whenever the restaurant is operating is perhaps our most important food safety requirement and critical to protecting diners.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Each year, the department trains about 35,000 restaurant supervisors in food protection at our health academy, awarding a wallet-size FPC certification card with the supervisor's photograph to those who complete the course and pass the exam.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Checking that an FPC holder is at the restaurant by reviewing the supervisor's FPC card is a key part of every food safety inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We understand that on occasion, the restaurant's

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: supervisor may not have their FPC card with them, leaving them unable to show that they have the required training.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: When that happens, the inspector attempts to contact the Health Academy for a database check to confirm the person is an FPC holder, but that process is imperfect, including because the records are deleted after 10 years, so older certificates are unavailable.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department supports the intent of the legislation, but is concerned that as drafted, the bill would require the department to maintain decades of electronic records and poses other operational hurdles.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We appreciate the discussion we have already had with the sponsor and look forward to discussing potential approaches with council.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Next, Introduction 1124 would require the FPC holder to renew their certification every five years.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We support the intent to enhance food safety protections and would like to work with the Council on the best ways to meet this objective.

chapters.summary: Schiff says Intro 189 would require photographs or video of violations cited during inspections. She says inspectors already document findings in reports and summonses and explain them to operators, but photographing and storing evidence could lengthen inspections and require significant data resources.
chapters.title: Schiff raises concerns about Intro 189 photo and video documentation

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Introduction 189 would require the department to include a photograph or video showing violations identified at the restaurant inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Restaurant inspectors review their observations with the restaurant operator throughout the inspection, including providing information about avoiding or correcting conditions that do not meet food safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They also document those findings in an inspection report and any summons that may be issued and provide those to the restaurant operator at the end of the inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Inspectors are New Yorkers'eyes in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Their findings are summarized in

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: into the letter grade posted in the restaurant window and diners who want inspection details can check our inspection website ABC Eats.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Results are also available on open data.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department is concerned that collecting photographs and video of the inspection would require

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: a longer inspection, especially for a restaurant failing to meet requirements and requiring photographic or video evidence of pest conditions, poor hygiene practices,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: food not kept at safe temperatures, and more, and require significant data resources to maintain millions of photographs and hours of video to transmit to Oath, post on ABC Eats, and store to meet record retention requirements.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing the bill with Council.

chapters.summary: Schiff says the 2001 Smoke-Free Air Act ended new tobacco bar permits and allowed existing bars to continue only in their existing locations to achieve attrition. She argues allowing tobacco bars to relocate or reopen after closing undermines the law and risks secondhand smoke exposure in nearby homes and businesses.
chapters.title: Schiff opposes Intro 947 tobacco bar relocation

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Introduction 947 would allow current tobacco bars to move and allow tobacco bars that had already closed to reopen, including in a new location.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The city's landmark Smoke-Free Air Act, passed by City Council in 2001, was enacted to end indoor tobacco smoking, prohibit the opening of new tobacco and cigar bars, and only allow existing bars to continue operating in their then-existing locations

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: under the permits they already had to enable the eventual attrition of these establishments.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The Smoke-Free Air Act ended the issuance of new permits for tobacco bars by the Health Department.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Allowing tobacco bars to relocate and resume operations after previously closing undermines the premise of the law.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: This rollback of our longstanding joint commitment to reducing secondhand smoke exposure

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: would put the decades-long progress the council and department have made to reduce tobacco-related health harms at risk.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Secondhand smoke exposure is not limited to the premises of the establishment.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Residential units and businesses nearby will also be affected.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: This is especially concerning because the decline in smoking in the city has now stalled, and we have seen widespread commentary in the media about a resurgence in the popularity of smoking.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We welcome the opportunity to discuss this further.

chapters.summary: Schiff says the department supports steps to make default food choices healthier and looks forward to strengthening Intro 405 on children's menus. On Intro 1094, she says DOHMH already requires reporting at higher Legionella levels and mandates corrective action at the same low level in the bill, and welcomes further discussion.
chapters.title: Schiff comments on Intro 405 nutrition standards and Intro 1094 Legionella reporting

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Next.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Introduction 405 would strengthen nutrition standards for children's menus in New York City restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department supports steps that shift the food environment to make default choices healthier and appreciates the prior conversations with the sponsor regarding this bill.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department looks forward to discussing how to further strengthen this bill in support of children's health.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Finally,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Introduction 1094 would require owners of cooling towers to report findings of Legionella bacteria at low levels to the department and to take corrective action.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The department already mandates owners to report results of Legionella bacteria to the department when those results show higher levels of bacteria, to maintain records of all sampling results for department review, and sets detailed requirements for corrective actions starting at the same low level

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: set out in the bill.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We look forward to discussing this proposed reporting requirement with you.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We are happy to take your questions.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks whether the 90% A-grade rate has always been the plateau. Schiff says restaurant grading launched in 2010, with 85% A grades in FY12, rising to 90% now, with some variation around COVID.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about 90% A-grade plateau

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a few questions and then I'm going to.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: hand it over to my colleagues and then come back.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So to give them an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, you said in your testimony that 90% of restaurants have an A.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Has that always been the plateau, or it's been higher, lower?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You want to just go through some of that?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So I'll say restaurant grading has been a huge success in New York City in promoting high food safety standards among city restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Last July, we celebrated our 15th anniversary of this program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And I did a little looking back in preparation for today.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And in FY12, we started the program in July 2010.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: In FY12, 85% of restaurants were posting A grades, and we're now at 90%.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And it stayed about that level.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's been a little bit higher before COVID, and we've been getting back up to that level.

chapters.summary: Schiff describes the grading system as an open-book exam with two chances to earn an A. If a restaurant does not earn an A on initial inspection, DOHMH returns for a re-inspection, usually aiming for about a month when fully staffed, and issues no summons if the restaurant earns an A.
chapters.title: Schiff explains re-inspection process for restaurants without an A

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When an establishment doesn't get an A, what is the process around that?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the program that we set up in 2010 for restaurant grading provides two opportunities for restaurants to get an A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And I will say that we think of the inspection as an open book exam to go along with those grades.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we list every condition that the inspector will look for in a checklist, and we make that available to restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We train them on it, and we encourage them to take that checklist and conduct a self-inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Every day, every week, as frequently as they can, so they are ready for that inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we go for an initial inspection, and if the restaurant earns an A at that time, they get that A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: When we issue an A grade at the time of inspection, there's no summons, there are no fines, all part of an incentive structure because we really want restaurants to be motivated to meet the city's high food safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If they don't earn an A at that inspection, we come back for a re-inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that's a really important moment for the restaurant to take a look at what we found that didn't result in an A, make those corrections, and then we come back and do that re-inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Again, if they earn an A at the time of inspection, they will get that A.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There's no summons.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There's no fines.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If it's not an A, then we give them, depending on the score, a B or a C, and that grade pending card that you've seen in some restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How much?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Time elapses between when they get less than an A and then you come back.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It can vary.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We will not come back before a week.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We want there to be enough time for them to come back.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it really does vary.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our goal is about a month when we're fully staffed.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about the ombudsman office for establishments. Schiff says the ombudsperson is a point of contact for restaurant owners, can review concerns, and can coach inspectors if issues arise; she says DOHMH also sends industry e-blasts with ombudsperson and customer service contacts.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about DOHMH ombudsman office and industry outreach

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you also, I understand you have an ombudsman office for establishments.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're not on fire.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do have an ombuds office, and that is a person, a point of contact person for restaurant owners if they have questions, if they have a complaint.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do get compliments also from the restaurant industry about inspections, and our ombudsperson is there to really be an internal advocate for that restaurant inspector, for that restaurant owner.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So if there is some concern about what happened at the restaurant, that person can review, talk them through it.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If it turns out that there was some issue with the inspector, then that inspector can be coached, corrected, and so on.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I would say the vast majority of what comes into the ombudsperson is.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Questions?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I don't think, like, when I was preparing for this hearing today, I didn't really know about the ombudsman office.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So if there's a way to get some information out, especially to the council members, and they can share it with their local businesses, and I think that would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And then it'll prevent us from doing legislation that...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is like not really needed or so?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I will say that we are routinely issuing information to restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do e-blasts to the entire industry.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And those often- You work with the Hospitality Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Yes, and those often include the contact information for the ombudsperson.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we also have a customer service office.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so we provide information about both of those contacts.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But we would be happy to get that information to you and have you support those outreach efforts.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The other thing, too, that just a suggestion that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When there's a problem with a restaurant that maybe, because a lot of the local council members have relationships with those businesses and they can maybe help to get them to a place where they get an A.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I think that would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Schiff says DOHMH regulates about 40,000 food service establishments, of which about 30,000 are restaurants, plus cafeterias, older adult centers, correctional facilities, and soup kitchens. She confirms complaints can be made through 311 and says DOHMH will check its website for additional complaint information.
chapters.title: Schiff details regulated food service establishments and complaint process

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And how many food service establishments does DOHMH currently regulate?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So food service establishments is a regulatory term that is bigger than restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There are about 40,000 of those in the city.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And there are about 30,000 of them are what we would consider restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Other than restaurants, you just want to give us the rundown of what it is that you inspect for the food grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we also have oversight responsibility for food service in cafeterias.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It could be school cafeterias.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It could be business cafeterias, older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Food service in correctional facilities, soup kitchens.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you just send us the list so that we know?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We will send you the list.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That would be awesome.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And somebody, if they have a complaint about an establishment, they can call 311, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is there anything on the website of DOHMH or just 311?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'll have to, we'll check our website to see what it says about complaints, but certainly at 311, either online or by phone.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Schiff says DOHMH inspected almost 21,400 restaurants in FY26, almost 21,000 in FY25, and just over 20,000 in FY24. She attributes the increase to ongoing recruitment and training of new inspectors.
chapters.title: Schiff reports inspection counts for FY24 through FY26

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So how many inspections did you guys conduct in each of the last three fiscal years?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So in FY26, we did almost 21,400.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Restaurants inspected, FY25 it was almost 21,000, and in FY24 just over 20,000.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So as you noted in your opening remarks, Chair, our recruitment efforts have been

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: rigorous and ongoing, and we are succeeding in bringing more inspectors on board, which is why you are seeing those numbers go up.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: met a group of new inspectors in training, a nice big group.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we are continuing to staff up.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm guessing that you don't have this with you, but if you can give us the number of the type of inspection, including the initial re-inspection compliance and complaint driven.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't have complaints, but I have FY26.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There were just over 16,000 initial inspections, almost 6,000 re-inspections, and just over 250 compliance inspections.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that was up from the year before, 15,000 initial inspections.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Schulman notes the FY2026 Mayor's Management Report says DOHMH inspected 71% of restaurants, below the 100% target. Schiff says about 8,800 restaurants were not inspected in FY26 and just under 500 had gone two or more years without inspection, while the department aims to inspect 100% and continues recruiting.
chapters.title: Schulman questions 71% inspection coverage and uninspected restaurants

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: According to the fiscal 2026 mayor's management report, DOHMH inspected 71% of the city's restaurants, roughly the same as in fiscal 2025, below the 100% target.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many restaurants went uninspected in fiscal year 2026, and how many have now gone more than two years without an inspection?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: In FY26, there were about 8,800 restaurants that were not inspected and just under 500 that had gone two or more years without an inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then another set of restaurants where we had attempted an inspection, the restaurant was closed and appeared to be out of business, but we would continue to inspect to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you think you're going to get to a place where it's,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: 95% and higher.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm just asking.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I mean, that's certainly our goal.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our goal is to inspect 100%.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I think you quoted 99 point something in your opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That is our goal, and we are continuing to recruit and really welcome the council's support to send us good candidates.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's a great job, a terrific way to serve your community.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Give us a job description, yeah, we can do that.

chapters.summary: Schiff says DOHMH inspects in every neighborhood and does not find any location especially hard to inspect. She describes the pest control program, restaurant pest-management training, and internal cross-referrals, and Schulman suggests coordinating with DOB on construction that affects nearby businesses.
chapters.title: Schiff says no locations are harder to inspect; discusses pest and construction coordination

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are there locations where it's more difficult for you to conduct inspections?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Like a location or something?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: No, we're all over the city.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We're in every neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have people working, you know, early and late.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I think there was, I think I saw someplace where it said a lot of issues have to do, you know, we have the highest rat population of any city in the country.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That it has something to do with vermin and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so do you work with any other?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I know we don't have the rat czar anymore, but do you work with any other agencies around that issue?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the health department, also within the environmental health division, has a pest control program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: A part of our training for restaurants is about pest management.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There are very specific requirements in our food safety rules about...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Controlling pests, maintaining conditions that reduce the risk of pests.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we also, you know, where there are extreme situations in a restaurant, which is not common, we can mostly handle the pest conditions within the Food Safety Bureau, but there are opportunities for internal

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: cross-referrals if we need to call in our pest program.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So what I'm also going to ask, because we're going to have a tremendous amount of construction to build new housing and everything else, and maybe work with DOB

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: around that issue when they have construction in various places, that especially now, like in my district, I have construction that's going to involve small businesses that are around where the construction sites are and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I'm going to...

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how DOHMH settled on the 1,000 CFU/mL mandatory notification threshold and whether it objects to lowering it to 10. Schiff says 1,000 is a longstanding CDC and research action level used by other jurisdictions, and notes DOHMH already requires corrective action at the same lower levels proposed in the bill.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about 1,000 CFU Legionella threshold and lowering to 10

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: to change gears here to talk about the cooling towers a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How did DOHMH initially settle on the 1,000 colony-forming units per milliliter threshold for mandatory notification?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That's an action level that has been established in the research literature, in longstanding CDC guidance, and is a level also that other jurisdictions follow.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does DOHMH have any objections to lowering the threshold to 10 CFU milliliters, as is the practice in other jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So our action levels are the same as what's in the bill and what I think you're referring to colleagues in Vancouver, Canada.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have the same action levels in New York City for owners to take corrective action, and we have very detailed specifications for what those action levels are.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The difference with Vancouver is that reporting requirement, although I will say that our programs are different, and our understanding is that in Vancouver as well, it is at 1,000 CFUs that those reports are made to the health department.

chapters.summary: Schiff explains that a 1,000 CFU result suggests a cooling tower operator may not fully control their maintenance program. She says a DOHMH unit follows up with buildings to ensure corrective action, sampling, and reporting, and notes the new 30-day sampling requirement will give operators more information.
chapters.title: Schiff describes DOHMH follow-up on Legionella notifications

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When DOHMH receives a notification from a cooling tower operator regarding the presence of potentially harmful levels of Legionella bacteria, what is the procedure for reviewing the notification?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So first, I want to just say that the way we think about that 1,000 CFU limit is that it's really an indication

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: that the cooling tower operator may not have full control over their maintenance program and plan.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And one of the reasons we were so supportive of your legislation in 2025, Chair, was that changing the

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: frequency of sampling from 90 days to 30 days, or 31 days technically, is that that was going to give operators so much more information about their control program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: As we discussed last month and last year, our regulations, the local law and our regulations, set out very specific requirements for owners of cooling towers on their maintenance program and plan.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And there's things that they need to do.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Every day or multiple times a week, weekly, bimonthly, monthly, biannually, annually.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're really maintaining their systems constantly.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But the new sampling regime is going to give them a lot more information about how that program is working to control the Legionella bacteria.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And I think we're still early days in seeing how that works.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But to answer your question, when we get those reports, we have a

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: There is a unit within the cooling tower program that does follow-up with those buildings, making sure that they take that corrective action, report the corrective action to us.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They have to then do sampling to see that that corrective action was successful.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They have to report that to us.

chapters.summary: Schulman says two outbreaks this year and hotter summers linked to climate change make new Legionella approaches necessary, and she plans expert testimony on her bill. Schiff says DOHMH looks forward to discussing how it would triage notifications if Intro 1094 passes.
chapters.title: Schulman discusses climate change, outbreaks, and triage under Intro 1094

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Since we've had these two outbreaks this year, which is troubling, we're trying to find some new ways to do this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And we are going to have experts, by the way, that are going to testify to my legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I assume somebody will be here from DOHMH when they testify.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But somebody's waving to me that they'll be here.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so we're trying to figure out different ways to get at this because the fact of the matter is because of climate change that

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: we're going to have more or potentially more Legionella because Legionella grows in warm atmospheres.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And we had a very hot summer last summer.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We had a very hot summer this summer.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that's what we're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So we'll work with you to figure it out, but I think we need to look at new ways to manage this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If this bill is enacted, how will DOHMH triage the notifications?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Will it change how the agency responds to a notification based off the levels of Legionella found in a cooling tower system?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we look forward to continuing to discuss the bill with you when we're still thinking.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: about those really important questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about Intro 1124's food protection certificate renewal and notes her chief of staff, a certified chef, suggested the idea. Schiff says every restaurant must have a supervisor with an FPC on site, the course is offered at the Health Academy and by authorized providers, and passing the exam earns a wallet-sized card.
chapters.title: Schulman asks what a food protection certificate is and how to qualify

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is, now I'm going to switch back, what I'm going to talk about my intro 1124, the food protection certificate renewal.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's an easy one.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is a food protection certificate and how does an individual qualify for one?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I want to just state for the record that

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: My chief of staff has a certificate.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: He's a certified chef.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And he came up with the idea of doing this because he felt that you need to know what's going on in the industry and all of that moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And it's good to do something like this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Other jurisdictions have it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But anyway, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Well, that's great.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So you...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: As I noted in my testimony, every restaurant is required to have a supervisor on site with a food protection certificate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And it's really the most important requirement that we have, and that's sort of intuitive, I think, that somebody trained in food protection supervising the operations in the restaurant would be critically important.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We offer the course at our health academy.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't know if you're, you can also take it from authorized third-party providers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So I don't know if your chief of staff took our course at the Health Academy on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's a long time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Okay, well, we've been offering it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's a great class.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I encourage everyone to take it, even for your own home cooking.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You may never, you know, you won't cook the same way again.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Know what temperature to cook my chicken to last night.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So at the end of that course, there is an exam.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And if you pass the exam, you get a card.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's a wallet-sized card, so easy to carry around.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Keep it in your wallet.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You'll have it with you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Please describe the material covered in the food protection course and what the final examination entails.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the course really covers, if you take it in person, it's every morning for four days, and then the fifth day it's a review session and exam.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it really covers all of the issues that are in our food safety rules and how to make sure that you are preparing, storing,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: serving food in ways that meets food safety protections to keep your diners safe.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Approximately how many people take the food protection course each year?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's about 35,000 every year.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Oh, wow.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Schiff says the in-person food protection course costs $114, the online course is free, and the review and exam cost $24. She says DOHMH offers free annual food safety training in person and online and will get back to Schulman on revenue generated.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about FPC fees, revenue, and continuing education

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What fees are associated with obtaining a food protection certificate, and how much revenue, if any, does DOHMH generate from this process?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the in-person course is $114.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The online course is free.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then to take the review course and exam, it's $24 at our health academy.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does DOHMH or another entity engage in continuing education opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: For food protection certificate holders as food safety practices evolve over time.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: new public health concerns emerge, such as foodborne pathogens?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do, and it's a well-timed question.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We are really in the middle.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Every year we offer a free food safety training program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We offer that in person in different boroughs, and we offer it online, and it's very popular.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Hundreds of restaurant operators come to it, and it is a chance to do exactly what you said, Chair, to refresh any new information in food safety science and remind people of restaurant workers of the most important

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: food safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We also bring in colleagues from other agencies to provide information and support services for the industry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: One question you didn't answer, how much revenue, if any, does the...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'm going to have to get back to you about that, yeah.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks questions for Council Member Santoso's Intro 908, including whether a digital database of FPC holders exists. Schiff says DOHMH maintains a database but records are kept for only 10 years, so older certificates may be unavailable, and that record limitations and the volume of 35,000 annual trainees are challenges.
chapters.title: Schulman asks whether DOHMH maintains a digital FPC database

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What specific amendment...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm going to ask some questions that Councilmember Santososo gave me for her introduction.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is a digital database of food protection certificate holders currently maintained?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do have a database.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Records are maintained for 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So this is one of the challenges that we would like to discuss with council about the bill, maybe even your chief of staff, depending on how long ago that person got their food protection certificate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we have been doing this for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We may not have that in the database.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So certainly looking back would be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And even just maintaining, as I said, we trained about 35,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So those are the kinds of things we'd like to talk with you about.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What operational changes, and again, this is her legislation, but yes, they're similar.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What operational changes would need to be made in order to create such a database or make it accessible to inspectors?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we're continuing to think about that, but as I noted, one issue is we can't look back.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Before 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then going forward, it would be quite an enormous database as we train 35,000 here.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about operational changes, whether AI could help, and the policy for missing FPC violations. Schiff says DOHMH is still studying it, cited about 2,800 violations in FY26 for no FPC holder on site, and says inspectors try database verification when possible; she confirms immigration status is not collected or maintained.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about FPC database access, AI, missing-certificate violations, and immigration status

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I hate to bring this up.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Would AI be helpful here?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we've got our best IT minds thinking about the

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But we look forward to talking with you about the details.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We are going to be having a hearing on AI in health care.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So just FYI there.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is there a standard policy for when a violation is given for a lack of food protection certificate on site?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And if so, what is that policy?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Yes, so having a person trained in food protection is perhaps the most important of all of the food safety requirements, and so it's a part of every one of our inspections.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: In FY26, we did cite it 28, we issued 2,800, about 2,800 violations for there not being a food protection certificate holder on site.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are there any circumstances currently in which DOHMH might try and verify whether or not someone has a food handler's license via the database as opposed to the physical card?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do do that, as I described in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We will when possible.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So, for example, it's a newer card, so it's going to be within the database.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And it's the database at the health academy, so the health inspector doesn't have access to that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So there are some technical things, but we do try to do that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What concerns, if any, does DOHMH have about creating, maintaining, or making more readily accessible this database?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So those are the concerns that I've noted.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you confirm that during the process of certifying a worker, their immigration status is not collected or maintained?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Not collected or maintained.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Oh, and I want to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how DOHMH establishes a violation existed when a restaurant challenges it, especially after correction, and asks about appeals. Schiff describes the inspection as a teachable moment with a checklist, printed report, and summons, and says restaurants can contest findings and present evidence at OATH.
chapters.title: Schulman questions how DOHMH proves violations when challenged and appeals

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to get the questions about the legislation out of the way.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This is about proposed intro 189, the photo or video evidence.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When a violation is challenged by an FSE, how does DOHMH establish that the violating condition existed at the time of inspection, particularly when the condition has since been corrected?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So first to note again, when the restaurant achieves an A grade at the time of the inspection, there is no summons as part of our overall

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: system, which is designed really to create a variety of incentives for the restaurant to meet those highest food safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we're talking about a restaurant that does not, to answer your question, does not get an A at the time of inspection, which means that we're finding food safety violations.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The inspection is, we consider it to be a teachable moment.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The inspector is there, and the restaurant, they walk through the restaurant with whoever the restaurant chooses to accompany the inspector.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We prefer a supervisor, but they can choose who that is.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we go step-by-step through that inspection checklist that we have shared with the restaurant because it's an open book exam and we want them to do their own self-inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And as we're going through, our inspector is describing what they're observing, why it meets or doesn't meet the food safety protection, and what needs to be done to bring that situation into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And they're recording that all along the way.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: At the end of the inspection, they review their overall findings with the restaurant operator.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They are carrying handheld printers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so at the end of the inspection, they are able to print out the inspection report and any summons right there on the spot for the restaurant owner to review.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: and sign.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The summons goes to oath, right?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The summons goes to oath, yes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is there another appeals process through oath if they want to appeal that?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If there is a summons issued, if it's not an A grade, then there is an opportunity for the restaurant owner to object to those findings and to bring in their evidence for why the inspector was wrong.

chapters.summary: Schiff says inspectors are trained to document observations in sworn summonses and detailed reports. She says DOHMH maintains written protocols and training materials and will follow up on exact inspection record retention periods; she says the department has some record of dismissed or reduced violations but has not recently analyzed trends.
chapters.title: Schiff explains inspector documentation and record retention practices

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What are our DOHMH inspectors currently required or instructed to document?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You just said that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How does the department determine whether a violation has been sufficiently documented to support the issuance of a notice of violation?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So that is a big part of our training program.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And the big cohort of new inspectors that I met last week or so were learning all of the different violations,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: trained in customer service to be able to deliver that teaching inspection, and also to document that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It is a legal document, and we do have to establish the conditions that meet the violation.
