utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is this one statement sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The summons that we issue is a sworn statement by the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They're putting in details of their observations, and then they're signing it at the end.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I think you mentioned this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: DOHMH maintains written protocols and training materials.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Governing this?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How long are FSE?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Inspection records retained.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You know, we meet the city's record retention program, and I will get back to you about exactly what that number is, because I don't want to get that wrong.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does the department track how often violations are dismissed, reduced, or otherwise resolved because of insufficient documentation or conflicting accounts of the inspection?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have some record of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And is there any trends that come out of that that you see?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I haven't looked at that in a long time, so I don't know, but others are looking at that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Curiosity.

chapters.summary: Schiff says inspectors already record detailed observations, such as counting mouse droppings, and questions whether photographs are needed for every violation. She says the bill's documentation requirement applies once an inspection reaches 14 or more points, but the score is unknown until the end, so the impact could be complex.
chapters.title: Schulman asks whether photo/video evidence would lengthen inspections and which violations benefit

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does DOHMH anticipate that taking photographs or video of cited violations would lengthen, you said that in your testimony,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: are there particular categories of violations for which photographs or video would be especially useful in demonstrating a public health risk?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: As I said, we do train the inspectors to make very detailed recordings of their observations.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: To give you an example, pest condition could be a common finding in a restaurant, especially one that's not getting an A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So there will be a summons.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And the inspectors are literally trained.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: To count mouse droppings that they observe and to record the numbers of mouse droppings that they have seen.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Do we also need a photograph of that?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The purpose of our documenting is to let the restaurant owner and Oath know about that observation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you know what percentage of FSE inspections annually would be affected by this bill's documentation requirements?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it would be any of the restaurant inspections where there isn't an A at the time of inspection, and so there is a summons.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Which would be like 10%.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It would be, you know what, we'll have to, there's some complexity to your question, but also.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We don't know until the end of the inspection what the score is going to be.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So I don't know at the beginning, right?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The bill applies to an inspection with 14 or more points.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That's because that's the cutoff for an A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: A is under 14.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We don't know at the start.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We only know at the finish.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I may be subject to documentation requirements for having taken that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Those photographs or videos anyway, so probably 100%, but we would have to do a little more thinking about that.

chapters.summary: Schiff says closing a restaurant is an extreme measure requiring multiple levels of supervisory review and is used only when conditions cannot be corrected before the end of an inspection. She says DOHMH gives owners detailed correction requirements and customer service support, and reopening time varies from next-day repairs to longer pest remediation.
chapters.title: Schiff explains restaurant closure and reopening process

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: It's not about a bill.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When you close a restaurant, which is very rare, but when you do, what's the process for them reopening?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because you talked about...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Like from a B to a C and that upgrade, but how does the closing work?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So closing a restaurant is something we hope not to do.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It is an extreme measure that we take only when we feel, based on the observations, that that restaurant cannot safely serve its customers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's not a decision that's made by the inspector.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The inspector reports back to the office to their supervisor, and there are multiple levels of supervisory review before we take that extreme action.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Any of the conditions, we call them public health hazards, that could be fixed by the restaurant before the end of the inspection, that won't result in a closure.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have them fix those conditions.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We want restaurants to stay open.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Where we feel that those conditions cannot be corrected before the end of the inspection, we will close that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we then provide very detailed information to the restaurant owner about the conditions that have to be corrected before they can reopen.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That's where our customer service office is really active, working with that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If they don't understand, if they have questions, if they need more guidance, we are there for them.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our goal is to get that restaurant open safely as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: About approximately how much time elapses in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It really ranges.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It depends on the conditions.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Some of the conditions cannot be fixed quickly.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If there is a severe pest infestation, you're going to need to plug up holes.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You're going to probably need to dispose of some food if we've found gnaw marks in some milk bags.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: of flour or something.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You're going to need to get pest-proof containers.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You're going to need a couple of extermination sessions.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it really varies on what we have seen.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If your refrigerators are not working, you can't hold food at a safe temperature, but you can get someone in there the next day and get those refrigerators repaired, that's going to be much faster.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how DOHMH enforces current local law on beverages offered with children's meals. Kim Kessler says these requirements are part of the regular inspection and enforcement process.
chapters.title: Schulman asks how DOHMH enforces existing children's meal beverage rules

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask about proposed intro 405, the healthy kids meals.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How does DOHMH currently enforce New York City's existing requirements concerning beverages offered with children's meals as codified in local law?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I think that's just part of the regular inspection process.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How does the agency currently monitor compliance with the existing children's meal requirements?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: It is similar.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: It is the same process.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are these requirements incorporated into routine restaurant inspections, complaint-driven inspections, or another enforcement process?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I believe they're part of the regular enforcement process.

chapters.summary: Kessler says childhood nutrition is a major priority and cites data that 5% of younger children and 10% of public high school students had no fruits or vegetables the previous day. She says the bill would allow whole milk because it is recommended for ages one to two, but DOHMH has concerns about added sugars in flavored milk.
chapters.title: Kessler discusses child nutrition data, whole milk, and flavored milk

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What does DOHMH's current public health data show about the nutritional challenges facing children in New York City, particularly with respect to fruit and vegetable consumption, added sugar, sodium, saturated fat, and childhood obesity?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: These are all areas of ongoing concern in New York City and a huge priority for us, the health department.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: Specifically for fruit and vegetable consumption, one of the things that I think is really promising about the legislation, which would require a fruit and vegetable to be served as part of all kids'meals, is that it really would help just normalize that as part of children's meals.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: Some of the more recent data that we have about this is that for kids between up to 13 years old, I think it's 5 to 13, it's 5% of kids who haven't had any fruits and vegetables in the day before.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And for public high school students, that's 10%.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: So that's just to give it an indication.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And certainly other nutrients of concern that would be limited by the proposed legislation, at least in chain restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: such as sodium and saturated fat, you know, those are just also things that there's too much consumption of in the American diet and for New Yorkers as well.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Believe me, I look at the labels and I'm like, what?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This is a little bit controversial, this question, but what is DOHMH's position on the consumption of whole milk by children?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: The legislation, the current draft of the legislation would allow for whole milk to be served.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And given that this kids meals could be consumed by kids of all ages and whole milk is actually recommended for kids between one and two, we think it makes sense for parents to be able to choose and for that to be available in restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is nonfat and low-fat milk healthier than whole milk?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I know there's this whole controversy around this.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I think we apply the New York City food standards for meals that are served in city meals, and those meals have an overall saturated fat limitation requirement.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I think, you know, whole low and reduced fat milk is what is promoted in city food standards for kids.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And this legislation is really thinking about the whole spectrum of age.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is DOHMH's position on flavored milk?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: We do have concerns about the sugars in flavored milk, and this legislation doesn't have limits on added sugars.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And so one way to reduce the amount of added sugars that would be available in kids'meals would be to make this for unflavored milk.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: Given just how much sugar kids are consuming, we think that's a good opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What procedures would DOHMH use to assess compliance with the nutritional limits for chain establishments, including calories, sodium, saturated fat, and fiber?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: The specific requirements that are in the proposed legislation for chain restaurants are ones that the FDA does require chain restaurants to disclose, which makes it feasible for that to become part of the inspection process.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And, you know, we look forward to discussing details of the enforcement process.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is the amended bill that the committee is hearing today enforceable from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: From our perspective, it is.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And I know that the legislation allows for rulemaking also, which would allow us to add more detail about if necessary.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks whether DOHMH has received relocation requests from tobacco bar operators and notes that some were displaced when landlords sold buildings during COVID. Kessler says she is not sure about specific requests and underscores the public health success of the Smoke-Free Air Act.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about tobacco bar relocation requests and COVID context

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, and now I'm going to ask about the tobacco bars, which I know is like a major issue for you guys.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Has DOHMH received requests from tobacco bar operators seeking to relocate due to financial hardship or other factors?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I just want to, for the record, say that

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: This bill came out of when COVID happened and there were landlords that sold buildings in which these establishments, because I know you're looking for attrition around these establishments.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so they were put out of business before their natural life course would go out of business.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So they're seeking this one time.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Transfer of the license and then the nutrition would start from that point.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Anyway, have you received requests, and if so, how were those requests handled, and was any form of assistance offered to these operators?

chapters.summary: Kessler says tobacco bars have declined from eight to five, consistent with the Smoke-Free Air Act's goal of reducing exposure. Dr. Talati says secondhand smoke contains cancer-causing chemicals, worsens asthma, and has no safe level, and that DOHMH receives thousands of complaints about secondhand smoke exposure.
chapters.title: Kessler and Talati defend Smoke-Free Air Act and secondhand smoke protections

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I'm actually not sure about specific requests.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I would just want to underscore what you just referenced and what the Deputy Commissioner spoke about in her testimony, just about the

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: shared public health success of the Smoke-Free Air Act, the aim of reducing exposure to secondhand smoke, which remains a huge public health concern,

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: and moving from eight of the tobacco bars that existed at the time of the legislation to five today is consistent with what would have been expected and a reduction of these hazardous businesses that have hazardous health consequences.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And because we do think it's important to just keep a front of mind in considering these issues and when weighing this legislation, I would also love my colleague, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: Achula Chalati, just to speak a bit more about secondhand smoke.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: So secondhand smoke, like you know, contains tar and cancer-causing chemicals.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: And so because of that, it lowers air quality, worsens asthma, but can also cause chronic disease.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: And there's no real safe level of secondhand smoke.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: And I think that's why we're concerned about anything that, you know, does not continue to reduce indoor smoking over time.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: And that's really why that was.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: The goal of the Smoke-Free Air Act.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: We also get thousands of complaints every year from New Yorkers about secondhand smoke exposure.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: So for any new location, I think we're not only concerned about the safety of the staff who work at that location, but also New Yorkers who live or work nearby and will be affected potentially on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, the legislation doesn't say carte blanche, that you can open up and that's that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I mean, they'd have to work with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I think we're talking about less than 10 of these places, to be honest.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks whether tobacco retail density is linked to adverse health outcomes at the community district level and whether DOHMH has data on complaints involving tobacco bars. Kessler says tobacco retail reduction is a core strategy, five tobacco bars currently operate, and DOHMH would welcome discussing amendments that preserve public health.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about tobacco retail density, complaints, and amendments

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Has, can you, what specific, wait, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you have evidence that tobacco retail density is associated with adverse health outcomes at the community district level?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we've analyzed that at the community district level.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: It is, I think, irrefutable that tobacco is of public health concern, and one of the core strategies in tobacco control is retail reduction.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: We want to reduce just the prevalence, availability, the normalization of the use of tobacco products, and that's consistent with other legislation around licenses that we've worked on together, as well as the Smoke-Free Air Act overall.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: And again, that's because of the evidence connecting tobacco with health harms.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you have data on complaints, inspections, violations, or other health-related concerns involving currently registered tobacco bars?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you know the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Achala Talati
utterances.text: I think we would have to double check specifically about tobacco bars.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you get back to us because that would play into a lot of this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many tobacco bars currently operate in the city, do you know?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: There are currently five operating in the city, and as mentioned, that is a reduction from the eight, consistent with the intention of reducing exposure to these businesses that have health harms.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Would you have specific amendments to make the bill workable for small businesses while preserving the public health objectives of the existing tobacco licensing framework?

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: I think we'd welcome the opportunity to discuss that further.

utterances.speaker: Kim Kessler
utterances.text: We would want to make sure that health is at the forefront of any considerations.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to turn it over to my colleagues now.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have other questions, but I wanted them to have the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So Councilmember Epstein is first.

chapters.summary: Council Member Epstein asks whether the 90% A-grade rate differs between takeout and sit-down restaurants, and whether violations are higher for takeout. Schiff says DOHMH does not have that distinction but will check, and Epstein says his office hears more complaints about takeout establishments and buffets.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for A-grade and violation breakdown by takeout versus sit-down

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Hi, good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You mentioned that 90% of restaurants have A ratings.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Does that break down by restaurants that are takeout or sit-down?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that a distinction between those A ratings?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We don't have that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can you get it?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I can look.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It'd be great if you let me know.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And just with some of the takeout restaurants, do you have data on how many of the violations you issued?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Are they higher percentage of violations for takeout restaurants, for sit-down restaurants?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We can take a look and see if we have that data.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, the reason I'm asking this is because we don't get a lot of complaints about health issues on restaurants unless it's related to a takeout establishment.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And we see kind of more, you know, with buffets, food being out, and kind of airborne illness.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're seeing higher percentages of that happening.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that, you know, it's only anecdotally.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering what you see internally.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I've not heard that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'll have to, I'll check with the team that takes in those complaints to see if they are seeing the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Of course, the same rules about food safety would apply, whether it's sit down or take out.

chapters.summary: Epstein describes takeout places in his district that have repeated inspections, violations, and shutdowns but keep reopening. Schiff says DOHMH has authority to act against owners unable to comply but exercises it extremely rarely, preferring technical assistance and an inspection history report; she will provide data on how often the authority is used.
chapters.title: Epstein raises repeat violations and DOHMH authority to shut problem establishments

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So there are a couple of takeout places in my district where there have been ongoing concerns, where there are...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: have been inspections, violations, shut down, and they just continue to reopen to a moment where if someone has ongoing violations, where a health department makes a determination that

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: that location or that establishment in that location can't continue to operate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do have the authority to take action against a restaurant owner who appears to be unable to comply with food safety requirements.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how often have you exercised that option?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Extremely rarely.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our goal is to bring restaurants into compliance.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we are much more likely to try to provide technical assistance to that restaurant owner to help them.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Come into compliance with the requirements.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have lots of tools for restaurant owners.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: For example, one we haven't talked about is we've developed what we call an inspection history report.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Any restaurant can get on our website, type in some information, their permit number or something like that, and get an individualized report that shows their last three years of history of repeat violations.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so that's our way of saying,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Here's something to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: These are things that you continue to do wrong.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we're really, our goal is, and we can work with SBS.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They also have a compliance team to bring that restaurant into compliance and to be able to operate.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: When how extremely rarely how often have you exercised that tool?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't have that number.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'd have to check.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could you check and get back to us on it?

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about recycling and trash issues around takeout locations and whether missing bins are a health department matter. Schiff says DOHMH inspects trash handling that could cause pests inside restaurants, but curb trash may involve another agency, and she will follow up for more detail.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about trash and recycling at takeout establishments

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And just just in this lane, we've also heard around kind of the food safety issue around.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Not having enough recycling and trash for takeout locations.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Have you heard that as an issue?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what does the health department do about ensuring cleanliness around and in front of the food safety establishment?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Depending on where the trash is, we will be doing an inspection of

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: maintaining trash in a way that especially prevents pest conditions in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But if you're talking about how they put trash out on the curb and so on, that may not be the health department.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So maybe we can follow up and get a little more detail about these issues and see where that falls.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if someone doesn't have a trash can or recycling bin in that takeout establishment, is that an issue that the health department will manage?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So restaurants do have to have containers to maintain their trash in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Council Member Wilson, a former server, describes restaurants using host alarms to stall inspectors and asks how DOHMH collaborates with industry on practical peak-service conditions. Schiff acknowledges some restaurants do this, says inspections are unannounced to see actual practices, and emphasizes ongoing training and education.
chapters.title: Wilson asks how DOHMH aligns inspections with real restaurant operations

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Council Member Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I was a server for 10 years at two prominent New York City restaurants.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: It's a great job and a great industry to work in.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But one of the restaurants I worked at, it's no longer there, but it had a good run.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: We had an alarm at the host.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: that would get pressed when the health inspector arrived to stall to get them to the kitchen so that the kitchen could get its, you know, make sure it was ready for the inspection.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So my question is, there are ways that restaurants practically run in the middle of food service that, you know, are often not.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: The way that the health inspector will see the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So how are you collaborating with the industry to ensure that you're scoring and looking for the,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: maintaining the safety of the food that also matches with the ways that a restaurant will practically run food service, like during a peak lunch shift or dinner shift?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do know that some restaurants will do what you just described.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our inspection is unannounced in an effort to see the actual practices of the restaurant, but some restaurants do as you say.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But it's part of why we continue to do training.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We know that restaurants want to keep their customers healthy and safe.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so there are a lot of things that we do to continue to educate restaurants so that they will know what is required to keep their customers safe.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how DOHMH manages inspection timing so restaurants do not lose shifts of income. Schiff says restaurants are not required to stop service, inspections are randomized from DOHMH's side and unannounced to restaurants, and the decision to pause service is the restaurant's.
chapters.title: Wilson questions inspection timing and lost service

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And you said they're unannounced, but when the health inspector shows up to a restaurant, that will shut down the service.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So how do you manage the timing of the inspection to ensure that they're not going to lose a full

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: shift or two worth of income, which we, of course, know can really make or break restaurants that often operate in the red?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Restaurants do not need to stop service.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: They don't need to, but it's like practically it's quite difficult to maintain it while there's an inspection going on.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So some restaurants choose to do that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It is not required, and we don't recommend it.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The timing is randomized from our point of view.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It is scheduled by us, but it is unannounced for the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Restaurants are working all the time, serving all the time, so we really can't inspect only when there is no possibility that they're serving food.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But that's a decision that the restaurant is making.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks how DOHMH ensures landlords of commercial food spaces are partners in hygiene and food safety. Schiff says DOHMH's relationship is with the permit holder but some obligations, such as pest-free property conditions, fall on building owners, and the department may cross-refer to its pest control program.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about landlord responsibilities and commercial tenant outreach

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: When you do the inspections, there are certain elements of the building that's controlled by the restaurant and others that are by the landlord that rents the space to the commercial tenant.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What are some ways that the health department ensures that landlords of buildings...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are active partners in maintaining hygiene and food safety, and how to ensure

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: make landlords aware of what their responsibilities are to commercial food tenants.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our relationship is with the permit holder, so the person that owns that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And certain of the requirements certainly have to do with facilities.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And so we would recommend that restaurant owners make sure that that lease and that relationship with the property owner is clear.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: In some certain circumstances, they may need cooperation with the property owner to make corrections if they are.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Building related, for example.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But our relationship is with the restaurant owner.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So the department does not do any types of trainings or outreach to commercial landlords that have leases with commercial food tenants?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It might depend on what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If there is a pest condition, as we were talking about before, some of those obligations are on the owner of the property.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So it may depend on exactly what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the owner of the property is responsible for maintaining that property in a pest-free state.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The restaurant would certainly be responsible for making sure that there are not...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Holes that allow the pests to move around their restaurant, whether there's an opportunity for our pest control program to intervene with that property manager, there may be, and sometimes we do that internal cross

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: reference that I was noting between our food safety program and our pest control program.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Narcisse says she previously owned a restaurant and an adult day care and asks about DOHMH's FY2027 food service inspection budget and inspector salaries. Schiff says the Food Safety Bureau budget is about $25 million, with about $20 million for personnel.
chapters.title: Narcisse shares industry experience and asks about inspection budget and payroll

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Council Member Nwasi.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And when I had a restaurant, we did not have the grade A, so that was a good thing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I wore many hats in my life.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But the supervision was always there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You had to take the classes, and I know how to handle my food before so I can check in the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But if you check restaurants, just like you check the adult senior daycare, which I had one,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It was just amazing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You're always on point when you come with the inspection.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I didn't know that restaurant was not getting the same love that we were receiving in social daycare.

utterances.text: So I want to say thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But now, what is the DOHMH fiscal 2027 budget for food service establishment inspection?

utterances.text: And how much is allocated to inspector salaries?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How much did DOH spend on inspectors'payroll fiscal 2026?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: The overall budget for our Food Safety Bureau is about $25 million, and about $20 million of that is for personnel.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how long restaurants sit on grade pending while contesting violations at OATH. Schiff says restaurants may keep grade pending cards while waiting for OATH hearings, and questions about how long that takes should be directed to OATH.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about grade pending duration and OATH delays

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How long do restaurants typically sit on grade pending?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because sometimes I see them for a while while contesting, if they're contesting at oath.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that being used to avoid posting a B or C for months?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I'm always questioning my head.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the restaurants have the opportunity to leave that grade pending card up while they're waiting for their oath hearing.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And how long that takes is really a question for oath.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: They have rules about being able to postpone and so on.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So I would refer your question to oath.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah, because they're pending for a while.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about the most common critical violations and what DOHMH does beyond fines, and how long a newly opened restaurant waits for inspection. Schiff lists vermin-proofing, harborage, food contamination, unsafe temperatures, and equipment maintenance, and says she will get back to Narcisse on new-restaurant inspection timing.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about common critical violations and new restaurant inspection timeline

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What is the most common critical violation citywide right now, and what is the department doing about it beyond issuing fines?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So some of our most common violations are

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: that the facility is not vermin-proof, there are harborage conditions, food is not protected from contamination, the food is held at unsafe temperatures, or

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: there's equipment that's not properly maintained.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do a lot of different things.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We are routinely sending out information to restaurants, referring them to the wide range of information we have on our website.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have annual refresher trainings like the one I mentioned that are underway.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Now we welcome restaurants to send multiple people to our health academy.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Many restaurants do that, and that's a great way to make sure that you're meeting the food safety requirements in your restaurant is to have multiple people.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: trained.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then as I said, every inspection is a teachable moment.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I hope that's what you experience.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That inspector is walking through describing everything that they are observing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How long does it take to receive the inspection if you just open a restaurant right now in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how long does it take?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If you open, yeah, a newly opened restaurant, how long will it take to get an inspection from the department?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: For a new restaurant, I'd have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't have that data with me.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member De La Rosa asks whether five-year recertification would help the 10% of restaurants without an A. Schiff says ongoing training could help but she does not know if it would reach 100% A grades; De La Rosa also asks whether the certification exam is available in multiple languages, and Schiff says the guide is in 36 languages but will check on the exam.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks whether recertification and language access can close A-grade gap

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Councilmember De La Rosa?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I had a question.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So we already heard 90% of restaurants have an A grade.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Do you believe that requiring the reapplication will solve for the 10% that is not an A grade?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Requiring the recertification.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You know, ongoing training and refresher training, it could be an important part of food safety.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But whether it would bring us to 100% of A's, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What do you see as the discrepancy between all of the restaurants that have the A's and the ones that don't?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like, what is the main...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: challenge?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Well, I would say that those most common violations would be something that the restaurants would look at.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And really, those restaurants that are not getting that A grade are just not, they're not meeting those high food safety standards that we set out in our health code.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And the grade is one among many incentive systems that we have to try to encourage restaurants to do that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then to take the opportunity to participate in all of that out.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: reach and education and training that we offer.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: The test for the food safety and protection or the certifications, are those offered in multiple languages?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Our guide, our inspection guide is offered in 36 languages other than English.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I have to check and see if literally the exam is in those languages or just the course review.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I've always brought up to the city in other hearings, you know, when you're not an English language, native English language speaker, you think in another language and you're actively translating.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So you study different and you test different.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So it's important, especially considering the diversity of the food of the city.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: That they're able to take these courses in their language if possible.

chapters.summary: De La Rosa asks how restaurants are notified when health or food safety rules change and whether renewal should be tied to major changes. Schiff describes public comment notices, industry emails, guidance materials, and compliance periods, but notes tying renewal to a single date would cause all FPC renewals to happen at once.
chapters.title: De La Rosa asks how restaurants learn of health code updates and five-year renewal timing

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I wanted to ask about, in your opinion, you know, when the health code is updated or the food safety regulations are updated, how do restaurants get notified that that update is happening?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And then does it make more sense to tie a reapplication to major changes or you all believe that the five years is sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: the five-year reapplication.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we periodically update the health code because food safety science evolves, and we will keep an eye on the model,

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: the FDA model food code, at least when we were confident that that was an evidence-based document, and continue to keep our food code, our health code, food safety requirements up to date.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: When we do that, we have many opportunities and moments when we notify the industry.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: First, when we put that rule out for public comment, we will send an email out to all restaurants because we want them to know that there are rules that the Board of Health is considering, and we want to hear from them what they think of those changes.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If the board adopts those changes, we then take another opportunity and let the industry know that the changes have been made.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We develop guidance materials that we will then distribute.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We will typically have a compliance period, giving us and the restaurants an opportunity to be ready to make those changes.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's an interesting question that you ask, whether that's the opportunity to update the food protection certificate.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I would want to give that a little more thought.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: One challenge off the top of my head is it means that everybody's renewal would have to happen at once.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So the thing.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: about, you know, everyone gets their food protection certificate at a different time, depending on when they take that course, that means that the renewals, five-year renewals, are also staggered.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: If we tie it to a particular moment that affects the entire universe, that means that everybody would be subject to a renewal at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So that might be a challenge, but we can give that a little more thought.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And one suggestion is also, I'm sure you all do this in some way or another, but also having folks on the ground, just because I know that, you know, and when we talk about tech and digital, the digital divide, there's some businesses that are very, you know,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: anti-tech, not because they want to be, but that's just who's running them, right?

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure that folks are on the ground, letting people know about these changes.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I think that's a good way to compromise on that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that is a part when the reason that we have a little lead time before we implement typically is because it is a chance for the inspector to talk through with the restaurant owner what's coming.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about DOHMH's hiring target for additional health inspectors and when full staffing is expected. Schiff says recruitment is active, the commissioner is enthusiastic and has promoted the job, and DOHMH wants to be fully staffed as soon as possible.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about inspector hiring targets and recruitment

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: According to the fiscal 2026 Mayors Management Report, DOHMH is working to hire additional health inspectors to meet safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What is the hiring target?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I know you talked about the new class.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And by what date does DOHMH expect to reach full staffing?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we do have a really active recruitment program, and again, we would welcome your help.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We want to be fully staffed as soon as we can, and we're really routinely looking for great candidates.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I'll say that our commissioner is very enthusiastic about this as well, and he's been out on inspections, he's met with our inspectors, and has been posting on his own social media to market what a great job this is.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how much DOHMH spent on inspector overtime in FY2025 and FY2026 and whether overtime is sustainable. Schiff says a few hundred thousand dollars, overtime is used to approach inspection targets but is not the goal, and barriers include science-degree requirements and no work-from-home option; she says funding is not the main issue.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about overtime spending, sustainability, and hiring barriers

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How much did DOHMH spend on inspector overtime in fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We spent a few hundred thousand dollars.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does DOHMH consider overtime a sustainable way to close the gap, and has it assessed whether heavy overtime affects inspection quality or consistency?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We do offer overtime as a way of meeting, getting closer to our inspection targets, but really we want to be fully staffed.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Fully staffed, okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What are the main barriers to hiring and retaining inspectors?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is there a salary issue?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is there...

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: You know, the qualifications for this job is you need to be a college graduate with a science major.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And there's no, there really is no work from home opportunity to be a restaurant inspector.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: It's a very hard job, but it's a really terrific job, great way to serve your community.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So we are actively recruiting, but it has been a challenge to fill these positions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How does the salary compare with other cities?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you have a sense?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does DOHMH believe it needs increased funding to hire more inspectors, or is current funding sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: This is really not a funding issue.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We have no issues with OMB processing.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We're just really actively recruiting, and that's why I keep saying, please send us good candidates from your communities.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Send us the job description.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'll get it out to my colleagues on the committee.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks what percentage of restaurants earn an A on initial inspection versus re-inspection, and about missing or obscured grade cards. Schiff says a bit over half earn an A initially and says grade posting is checked in routine inspections, complaints, and sweeps, with just over 870 violations issued in FY26.
chapters.title: Schulman asks initial vs. re-inspection A rates and grade posting enforcement

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: A restaurant has two chances to earn an A in every inspection cycle.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If it doesn't earn an A on the first inspection, it's scored but ungraded.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: An inspector then goes back to the restaurant unannounced and the re-inspection is graded.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What percentage of establishments earn an A on the initial inspection versus re-inspection?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: A bit over half get that A at the first inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: What percentage of the staff we...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Let me do that again.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does the department have data on how often posted grades are missing, obscured, and not displayed as required?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: By the way, I have a food place in my district that has no...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Nothing in their window or inside, but we'll talk about that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And how is posting enforced?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So first we'll follow up with you to get the details about that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we do inspect for grade card posting violations, we would generally call that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: That's part of every routine inspection.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We will respond to complaints about that.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And we do sometimes do grade card sweeps, we call them, to see that restaurants are posting their grade card.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I can tell you that in FY26, we issued just over 870 violations.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks what happens when a restaurant with a B does not appear at its OATH hearing and how long that B stays posted. Schiff says the grade becomes final after the hearing opportunity and DOHMH returns in the next cycle, within a few months when fully staffed, to give another chance at an A.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about OATH no-shows and how long a B grade remains

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I have, what happens when they have an oath hearing and they don't show up to it?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I really wouldn't refer your oath questions to oath, but that is a default when you do not appear.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, let me ask it in the sense of DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They have a B, right?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They have a B.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They had an oath hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: They didn't show up to the oath hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How long does that B stay up there?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because B is not great either.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In terms of, you know, people, like, using the premises and all that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: stuff and using the restaurant or bakery or whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So is there anything else that you guys can do there to help them get to an A or?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: So once that grade becomes final, after that opportunity for the hearing, whether they appear or not, they've had that opportunity for the hearing, the grade becomes final.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And then we will go back for their next cycle.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And that's their next chance to get the A grade.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: How long is that cycle?

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: And when we're fully staffed for a B, we should be back there within a few months.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact protocol, so I'd have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: But we do that for those same reasons.

utterances.speaker: Corinne Schiff
utterances.text: We want the restaurant to have a new opportunity to get an A grade.

chapters.summary: Schulman praises DOHMH for being extremely prepared and thanks the department and inspectors for their work protecting the city. She announces a five-minute break before public testimony.
chapters.title: Schulman thanks DOHMH and announces five-minute break

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to also say, because, you know, in the past I've talked about there have been times when we've had hearings that I've complained that DOHMH wasn't prepared, but you're extremely prepared today.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I appreciate all the responses and for all the things that you are doing to keep our city safe, because as you know, people are getting sick all over the country around food pathogen issues and all kinds of stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And we really appreciate the job that you do, that the inspectors do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I wanted to, you know, when I have a criticism, I'll make it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But when I have a...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I have a compliment to get that, too.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So please let the commission and whoever's watching from City Hall, they're doing a great job at DOHMH.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And thank you guys very much for everything that you do.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And we'll circle back on the other stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: We're going to take a five-minute break and then do public testimony.

chapters.summary: Schulman opens public testimony, reminds attendees that decorum must be observed, and explains rules for witness testimony, written submissions, and no video or audio recordings at the witness table. She says each speaker has two minutes and calls the first panel of Charlton Smith and Carmen DeLeon, while acknowledging Pace University students in the room.
chapters.title: Schulman opens public testimony and sets two-minute rule

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Oh, it's...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, everyone, we will now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present video or audio recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recording to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic and the attached legislation.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If you have testimony that is longer than two minutes, please, you can submit it to...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You can submit it online and just do a summary of what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Within 72 hours of the adjournment of this hearing, audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And now I'll call up the first panel, Charlton Smith and Carmen DeLeon.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I also, before we start, I want to acknowledge that we have students here from Pace University who've come here to see how government works, so thank you for coming today.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You came to a good hearing, actually, to do that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, I can already tell you this is going to be longer than two minutes, so summarize what you're going to say.

chapters.summary: Carmen DeLeon, president of Local 768, says public health sanitarians and the Bureau of Food Safety face a staffing shortage and low salaries. She says the union will conduct salary metrics and raises concerns about physical and verbal assaults during inspections, calling Intro 189's documentation process impractical and redundant.
chapters.title: Carmen DeLeon of Local 768 raises inspector shortage, salary, and safety concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: We know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: So I am Carmen DeLeon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: I am, as always, the president for right now of Local 768.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: I represent many of the health care members throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: The public health sanitarians and the Bureau of Food Safety is covered by our local.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: So three points that I want to make.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: One of them is that there is a shortage of public health sanitarians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: With that being the Academy, the Bureau of Food Safety, we've had many issues throughout the years of my tenure of six years, and we haven't really gotten to look at that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: The second thing, of course, is the salary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: We haven't done metrics, so we are, after this, we're going to do metrics on salaries based on cities with the same type of cost of living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: And then the other thing is more pointedly to Intro 018.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: We have some serious concerns around safety and health for our members who have been physically and verbally assaulted during inspections.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: So there is that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: And then there's...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: one of my members when I was talking about this to get kind of some feedback was that the process that's being asked for in particular in 0189 is actually impractical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: It is a redundancy of processes that are already in place.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Is that the video one?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I was just figuring out which letter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carmen DeLeon
utterances.text: 0189, and I'm now going to turn it over to my executive vice president, Charlton Smith.

chapters.summary: Charlton Smith, Executive Vice President of Local 768 with 24 years at DOHMH, opposes Intro 189. He argues mandatory photo or video documentation for every cited violation would create administrative burdens, privacy risks, inspector distraction, safety and confrontation risks, data storage issues, inconsistent enforcement, and over-reliance on visuals, and he urges the Council to retain the existing discretionary framework.
chapters.title: Charlton Smith of Local 768 opposes Intro 189 photo/video mandate

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: My name is Charlton H.L.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: Smith.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: I'm currently the Executive Vice President and Grievance Rep for Local 768.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: I'm also, I have 24 years of service with New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, Bureau of Food Safety and Community Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: Including eight years as a public health sanitarian and 16 years as an associate public health sanitarian.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: As a dedicated public health professional with over two decades of field experience inspecting New York City food service establishment and in my capacity representing the frontline public health sanitarists of Local 768,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: I write to express serious concerns regarding Intro 189.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: While intended to increase transparency, making photographic or video documentation mandatory for every cited violation introduced severe operational safety and legal challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: that will undermine the efficacy of the inspection process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlton Smith
utterances.text: The current system allows inspectors to submit photos on a case-by-case basis, such as documenting layouts during pre-operational inspection, which do not carry notices of violation.

chapters.summary: Michael Davoli of the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network opposes Intro 947, saying it would undermine the Smoke-Free Air Act's attrition strategy and risk more tobacco saturation. chapters.summary: Virginia Villa of the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council supports Intro 1094. She describes a summer hotel case where Legionella levels were below the 1,000 CFU reporting threshold, so workers and guests were not notified and remediation only followed arbitration; she says lowering the reporting threshold to 10 CFU would improve transparency and protect workers and guests.
chapters.title: Virginia Villa of Hotel Trades Council supports Intro 1094 Legionella reporting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: My name is Virginia Villa, and I'm the Deputy Research Director at the Hotel and Gaming Trades Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: I'm here to testify in support of Intro 1094 today, which would be a crucial improvement to our city's public health and safety protocols.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Earlier this summer, HTC members were put in a precarious situation when a hotel was found to have high levels of Legionella, but they were not notified until the union got involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Because the levels did not meet the reporting threshold of 1,000 colony-forming units per milliliter, there was no requirement for reporting or remediation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Workers and guests were subsequently left in the dark.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Only after arbitration did the hotel agree to remediation, and still then the test showed that the hotel's Legionella density had increased four times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa

utterances.text: Under city law, immediate action and reporting to the city is only required if the rates exceed 1,000 of those colony forming units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: And there was nothing else the city could do in this case.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: Under the current rules, workers and guests were left vulnerable and uninformed to the potential health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: The current system in place to protect workers and guests had its hands tied by these numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
utterances.text: This legislation would establish a reporting requirement for results of 10 colony forming units per milliliter or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Virginia Villa
